paper_inconsistencies.printed: 501 recruited; 6 failed an attention check; Experiment 2 excluded 123 + 26 = 149; F1,490 (Experiment 1 ANOVA); t343 (Experiment 2 after exclusions); t495 (no exclusion)
paper_inconsistencies.check: 501 - 6 = 495; 495 - 149 = 346; the degrees of freedom imply N = 494 (F1,490 = N - 4), 345 (t343 = N - 2) and 497 (t495), so 1 and 4 participants are unaccounted for; 149 / 501 = 29.7% ('30%', p. 6) matches. The Student df of t206 + t226 (436 participants in the four groups) cannot reach the ANOVA N of 494 either (Welch df or unreported subsets). No cell n is printed, so none of this can be resolved
paper_inconsistencies.used: arm n_paper = 501 (recruited); no analysed n served; target cells carry no n

charity.text: Frank Mulberry is the owner of a large chain of ‘Mulberry’s’ department stores located throughout the Midwest. Recently, Mulberry donated several million dollars to a local children’s hospital in Omaha, Nebraska, where his company is based. Mulberry donated the money because he knew that the good publicity would boost the reputation of his company and get more people to come to his stores.

advertising.text: Frank Mulberry is the owner of a large chain of ‘Mulberry’s’ department stores located throughout the Midwest. Recently, Mulberry invested several million dollars in an extensive advertising campaign in Omaha, Nebraska, where his company is based. Mulberry invested the money because he knew that the good publicity would boost the reputation of his company and get more people to come to his stores.

charity_cf.text: Frank Mulberry is the owner of a large chain of ‘Mulberry’s’ department stores located throughout the Midwest. Recently, Mulberry donated several million dollars to a local children’s hospital in Omaha, Nebraska, where his company is based. Mulberry donated the money because he knew that the good publicity would boost the reputation of his company and get more people to come to his stores. Keep in mind that if he wanted to, Mulberry could have instead invested the money in advertising. This would have also increased the reputation of his company, but none of the money would have gone to charity.

advertising_cf.text: Frank Mulberry is the owner of a large chain of ‘Mulberry’s’ department stores located throughout the Midwest. Recently, Mulberry invested several million dollars in an extensive advertising campaign in Omaha, Nebraska, where his company is based. Mulberry invested the money because he knew that the good publicity would boost the reputation of his company and get more people to come to his stores. Keep in mind that if he wanted to, Mulberry could have instead donated the money to charity. This would have also increased the reputation of his company, but all of the money would have gone to charity.

charity.text: Daniel P. works as a promoter of charitable events. His organization handles the planning, promotion, and execution for major fundraising drives to raise donations for charity. Daniel P.’s organization is a for-profit company. After all of the organizational costs have been settled, he and his staff take a percentage of the remaining funds. Therefore, the more money that is earned for the charitable cause, the more profits go to Daniel P. and his staff.

Now, imagine that you are the head of a large charitable organization. You are planning a fundraising drive and you need to decide whether or not you will hire Daniel P.’s company or instead, whether you will go with an alternative promoter.

Listed below are a number of possible outcomes for the fundraising drive, including how much money will go to your charity and how much will go to the promoter (either Daniel P. or an alternative promoter). For each one, please indicate whether you would hire Daniel P. or the alternative promoter.

corporate.text: Daniel P. works as a promoter of corporate events. His organization handles the planning, promotion, and execution for major fundraising drives to raise seed money from investors. Daniel P.’s organization is a for-profit company. After all of the organizational costs have been settled, he and his staff take a percentage of the remaining funds. Therefore, the more money that is earned for the corporate cause, the more profits go to Daniel P. and his staff.

Now, imagine that you are the head of a large company. You are planning an investor fundraising drive and you need to decide whether or not you will hire Daniel P.’s company or instead, whether you will go with an alternative promoter.

Listed below are a number of possible outcomes for the fundraising drive, including how much money will go to your company and how much will go to the promoter (either Daniel P. or “other organizer”). For each pair of options, please indicate whether you would hire Daniel P. (A) or the other organizer (B) assuming the details provided.
